pathophysiology.summary: Dengue is the most widespread mosquito-borne viral infection in India, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, with large seasonal outbreaks during and after the monsoon. Four dengue virus serotypes circulate; infection with one gives lasting immunity to that serotype only, and a second infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe disease because cross-reacting antibodies can enhance viral entry into immune cells. The illness passes through three phases. The febrile phase lasts two to seven days, with high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, rash and a positive tourniquet test. Around the time the fever settles, a minority of patients enter the critical phase, usually lasting 24 to 48 hours, in which immune-mediated injury to the vascular endothelium causes plasma leakage. Fluid moves out of the circulation into the pleural and peritoneal spaces, the haematocrit rises, the pulse pressure narrows and, if leakage is not matched by careful fluid replacement, shock develops. Thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction and coagulopathy contribute to bleeding, and prolonged shock leads to organ injury including hepatitis, myocarditis and encephalopathy. In the recovery phase leaked fluid is reabsorbed, so continued intravenous fluid at this stage causes overload and pulmonary oedema. India's national guideline classifies patients as dengue without warning signs, dengue with warning signs and severe dengue, and bases treatment on this grouping, serial haematocrit and clinical response. There is no antiviral treatment; outcomes depend on recognising warning signs early, giving isotonic crystalloid in measured, tapering steps, avoiding aspirin and other anti-inflammatory drugs, and not giving prophylactic platelet transfusions (NCVBDC 2023).
keyMechanisms: Secondary infection with a different serotype increases the risk of severe disease through antibody-dependent enhancement.
Endothelial dysfunction in the critical phase causes plasma leakage, a rising haematocrit and shock (NCVBDC 2023, p. 15).
Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy contribute to bleeding.
Fluid reabsorption in the recovery phase causes overload if intravenous fluids continue (NCVBDC 2023, p. 28).

symptoms: Bleeding from gums or nose, black stools or heavy menses
physicalSigns: Positive tourniquet test (10 or more petechiae per 2.5 cm²) (NCVBDC 2023, p. 19)
Postural hypotension (systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more)
Narrow pulse pressure below 20 mmHg (shock) (NCVBDC 2023, p. 16)
redFlags: Warning signs: persistent vomiting, abdominal pain or tenderness, lethargy or restlessness, mucosal bleeding, syncope, fluid accumulation, liver enlarged more than 2 cm, rising haematocrit with rapidly falling platelets (NCVBDC 2023, p. 15)
Pulse pressure 20 mmHg or less, cold extremities or hypotension: shock
Severe bleeding
Aspartate or alanine aminotransferase 1000 U/L or more, or Glasgow coma score below 9: severe dengue (NCVBDC 2023, p. 20)
Breathlessness during fluid therapy (overload)
precipitants: Urban water storage that breeds Aedes
Previous dengue infection (risk of severe secondary infection)
Infancy, pregnancy, older age, diabetes, hypertension and kidney disease (higher-risk groups)

clinicalManagement.title: Classify and decide where to treat
actions: Classify as dengue without warning signs, with warning signs, or severe dengue (NCVBDC 2023, p. 15).
Take a baseline haematocrit before fluids where possible, but do not delay fluids for it (NCVBDC 2023, p. 35).
Admit children with warning signs and all patients with severe dengue (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 25–26).

branches.condition: No warning signs, tolerating oral fluids
actions: Manage at home with oral fluids and paracetamol; review daily and return at once with any warning sign.

clinicalManagement.title: Dengue with warning signs: measured crystalloid
actions: Give 7–10 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or Ringer's lactate) over 1 hour, using ideal body weight in obesity, and reassess hourly (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 36–37).
If improving, taper: 5–7 mL/kg/h for 2–4 h, then 3–5 mL/kg/h for 2–4 h, then 2–4 mL/kg/h for 2–4 h; stop by 24–48 h (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 36–37).
Target urine output about 0.5 mL/kg/h (NCVBDC 2023, p. 35).
Second bolus 10 mL/kg over 1 hour; if still not improving, manage as severe dengue (NCVBDC 2023, p. 36).
Suspect bleeding: whole blood 10 mL/kg or packed red cells 5 mL/kg (NCVBDC 2023, p. 36).

clinicalManagement.title: Severe dengue with shock
actions: Compensated shock: crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg over 1 hour, then 7–10, 5–7, 3–5 and 2–3 mL/kg/h in steps over 24–48 h (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 39–40).
Hypotensive shock: 20 mL/kg crystalloid or colloid over 15 minutes, then 10 mL/kg/h for 1 hour and taper (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 40–41).
Manage refractory shock in the intensive care unit (ICU) with inotropes after excluding bleeding, cardiogenic and septic causes (NCVBDC 2023, p. 41).
Repeat boluses 10–20 mL/kg over 15–30 minutes (maximum 500 mL per bolus), up to three in total (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 40–41).
Transfuse whole blood 10 mL/kg or packed red cells 5 mL/kg (NCVBDC 2023, p. 40).

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care and what to avoid
actions: Paracetamol for fever; avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs, intramuscular injections, diuretics in the leakage phase, corticosteroids for shock and hypotonic fluids (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 25–28, 34).
Do not give prophylactic platelet transfusions; transfuse platelets for bleeding, or consider below 10,000/mm³ without bleeding (NCVBDC 2023, pp. 41–42).

pathophysiology.summary: Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for stroke, heart attack, heart failure and chronic kidney disease in India, yet most affected adults are undiagnosed, untreated or uncontrolled. Sustained elevation of blood pressure reflects increased peripheral vascular resistance, often with excess salt intake, overweight, physical inactivity, harmful alcohol use, tobacco and ageing, and with activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic systems. Over years, raised pressure damages arterial walls, accelerates atherosclerosis, thickens the left ventricle and injures the small vessels of the brain, kidney and retina. Because the condition is usually symptomless until complications occur, control depends on screening every adult and on simple, reliable treatment that primary health workers can deliver at scale. The India Hypertension Control Initiative, run with the national programme for non-communicable diseases, uses a drug- and dose-specific standard protocol: amlodipine is started first, telmisartan is added and increased, amlodipine is increased, and chlorthalidone is added last, with blood pressure re-measured every 30 days and adherence checked before each step. A single protocol with a short list of medicines simplifies supply, training and follow-up, and supports free medicines at government health centres. The protocol defines who needs immediate referral, such as very high readings or raised creatinine, and adapts treatment for diabetes, previous heart attack or stroke, chronic kidney disease and women who are or may become pregnant, in whom telmisartan, other renin–angiotensin blockers, chlorthalidone and statins are avoided. Lifestyle measures, especially salt reduction, are part of every step (India Hypertension Control Initiative protocol).
keyMechanisms: Raised peripheral resistance with salt excess and renin–angiotensin and sympathetic activation sustains high pressure.
Chronic pressure load damages arteries and accelerates atherosclerosis.
Target-organ injury affects the brain, heart, kidney and retina.
Calcium-channel blockade, angiotensin-receptor blockade and thiazide-like diuresis lower pressure by complementary mechanisms (IHCI protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Stepwise drug protocol
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Re-measure every 30 days; check adherence before each step
actions: Step 1: amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
Step 2: add telmisartan 40 mg once daily.
Step 3: increase telmisartan to 80 mg.
Step 4: increase amlodipine to 10 mg.
Step 5: add chlorthalidone 6.25 mg.
Step 6: increase chlorthalidone to 12.5 mg.
If still uncontrolled with confirmed adherence after step 6: refer to a specialist.
Use enalapril 5 mg, intensified to 10 mg (IHCI protocol).
Use a calcium-channel blocker only; no telmisartan, chlorthalidone, ACE inhibitor or statin; refer if uncontrolled at the intensified dose.

clinicalManagement.title: Special groups
actions: Diabetes: treat per the diabetes protocol with a target below 140/90 mmHg.
Heart attack in the last 3 years: add a beta-blocker to amlodipine from the start.
Any previous heart attack or stroke: low-dose aspirin 75 mg and a statin.
Chronic kidney disease: an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker is preferred after specialist opinion with close monitoring.

title: Type 2 diabetes (India adaptation, Asian BMI cut-offs)

findings: Diagnostic criteria, screening, drug doses and renal metformin rules checked against ICMR 2018 pages cited.

pathophysiology.summary: Type 2 diabetes affects a very large number of adults in India and often begins at a younger age and lower body weight than in many other populations. Asian Indians tend to have more abdominal and visceral fat, more insulin resistance and a smaller reserve of insulin-secreting beta cells for a given body mass index, which is why ICMR uses lower thresholds — a body mass index of 23 kg/m² or more, or a waist above 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women — as risk factors for screening. The disease develops when insulin resistance in muscle, liver and fat is no longer matched by insulin secretion; beta-cell function declines progressively, so most people need more medicines over time. Chronic hyperglycaemia damages small blood vessels in the retina, kidney and nerves and accelerates atherosclerosis in large arteries, causing heart attack, stroke and peripheral arterial disease, while foot ulcers and infections follow neuropathy and poor circulation. Diagnosis rests on fasting plasma glucose, a two-hour oral glucose tolerance test or HbA1c, confirmed by a second test. ICMR recommends screening everyone over 30 years and earlier with risk factors, setting an HbA1c target below 7% for most people with individualisation, and starting metformin as the first drug unless contraindicated, with sulphonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors or SGLT2 inhibitors as preferred second-line choices and insulin when hyperglycaemia is severe or oral treatment fails. Structured annual screening for eye, kidney, foot and cardiovascular complications and education on diet, physical activity and hypoglycaemia are central to care (ICMR Guidelines for Management of Type 2 Diabetes 2018).
keyMechanisms: Insulin resistance in muscle, liver and fat with progressive beta-cell decline.
Asian Indians develop diabetes at lower body mass index with more visceral fat (ICMR 2018, p. 7).
Chronic hyperglycaemia causes retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.
Accelerated atherosclerosis causes heart attack, stroke and peripheral arterial disease.

evidenceAudit.scope: Postpartum haemorrhage prevention and treatment in India.
findings: Indian context checked against MoHFW Dakshata 2015 and ANC 2010; regimens carried from WHO 2025 as cited in Marifa's existing PPH topic.
unverifiedSections: WHO 2025 section locators were not re-opened in this task (the WHO page required user permission); they follow Marifa's existing PPH topic.

pathophysiology.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in India, and most deaths occur within hours of birth, often in women who had no recognised risk factors. Normally, after the placenta separates, the interlacing muscle fibres of the uterus contract and compress the spiral arteries that supplied the placental bed, controlling bleeding within minutes; this is why uterine atony, failure of the uterus to contract, causes most haemorrhages. Other causes are retained placenta or fragments, genital tract trauma and coagulation disorders, remembered as tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin. Anaemia, which is common in Indian women, reduces the reserve to tolerate blood loss, so women decompensate earlier and at smaller volumes. Prevention rests on giving a uterotonic to every woman immediately after birth as part of active management of the third stage of labour, together with controlled cord traction and uterine massage, a set of skills that India's Dakshata programme trains labour-room staff to perform. Where oxytocin cannot be kept cold, heat-stable carbetocin or oral misoprostol are alternatives, and India's community misoprostol programme extends prevention to home births. Treatment is time-critical: recognise excessive bleeding early, call for help, massage the uterus, give oxytocin, give tranexamic acid as early as possible and within three hours of birth, restore circulating volume, examine for the cause and escalate to second-line uterotonics, mechanical or surgical measures and transfusion. Delays in recognising haemorrhage, in reaching a facility able to transfuse and in escalating care drive deaths, so referral planning and blood availability are part of the pathway (WHO 2025; MoHFW Dakshata 2015).
keyMechanisms: Myometrial contraction compresses placental-bed vessels; atony causes most haemorrhage.
Causes: tone (atony), tissue (retained products), trauma and thrombin (coagulopathy).
Anaemia lowers the reserve, so decompensation occurs at smaller losses.
Uterotonics restore contraction; tranexamic acid reduces fibrinolysis.

title: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia (India adaptation, Pritchard regimen)

evidenceAudit.scope: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia in India: detection, Pritchard regimen, blood pressure and delivery.
findings: Magnesium regimen checked against the Dakshata checklist; thresholds against MoHFW ANC 2010.
unverifiedSections: No Indian source was opened for IV labetalol or hydralazine doses; the Update in Anaesthesia regimen used in Marifa's eclampsia topic is carried over.

pathophysiology.summary: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia are major causes of maternal and perinatal death in India. Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy-specific disorder that originates in the placenta. In normal pregnancy, trophoblast cells remodel the maternal spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels; in pre-eclampsia this remodelling is incomplete, the placenta becomes poorly perfused and releases anti-angiogenic factors into the maternal circulation. These factors injure the maternal endothelium throughout the body, producing hypertension, protein leak through the kidney, and in severe disease damage to the brain, liver, kidneys, blood clotting and lungs. Cerebral endothelial dysfunction and loss of autoregulation can cause severe headache, visual disturbance and convulsions, which define eclampsia. Liver involvement causes epigastric pain and the HELLP syndrome, and placental insufficiency restricts fetal growth and can cause abruption and stillbirth. MoHFW defines hypertension in pregnancy as systolic 140 mmHg or more and/or diastolic 90 mmHg or more on two readings at least four hours apart, and pre-eclampsia as hypertension with proteinuria. Magnesium sulphate is the anticonvulsant of choice to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures; India uses the Pritchard regimen, a combined intravenous and intramuscular loading dose followed by intramuscular maintenance doses, because it can be given safely at primary and first referral units with simple bedside monitoring of reflexes, breathing and urine output. Where the full regimen cannot be given, the loading dose is given and the woman is referred. Severe hypertension is lowered to protect the mother, and delivery is the definitive treatment. Low-dose aspirin and calcium supplementation reduce risk in women at high risk (MoHFW antenatal guideline 2010; Dakshata MgSO4 checklist; WHO 2013).
keyMechanisms: Incomplete spiral-artery remodelling causes placental hypoperfusion.
Anti-angiogenic factors cause widespread maternal endothelial injury.
Cerebral endothelial dysfunction causes headache, visual symptoms and eclamptic convulsions.
Magnesium sulphate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures (WHO 2013).

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis of severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia
actions: Loading: 4 g of 20% solution IV slowly over 5 minutes, plus 5 g of 50% solution deep IM in each buttock with 1 mL 2% lignocaine (Dakshata checklist).

Before each dose, check the knee jerk, respiratory rate and urine output; keep 10% calcium gluconate 10 mL ready as antidote (Dakshata checklist).
Give 2 g of 20% solution IV slowly over 5 minutes (Dakshata checklist).
Give the loading dose and transfer immediately (WHO 2013).

clinicalManagement.title: Control severe hypertension

Monitor blood pressure every 15–30 minutes until below 160/110 mmHg.

clinicalManagement.title: Plan delivery
actions: Delivery is the definitive treatment; expedite for severe pre-eclampsia at term or remote from term (WHO 2013).
Continue antihypertensives postpartum if treated in pregnancy or for severe postpartum hypertension (WHO 2013).
